metadata.title: Electrical Fundamentals & Aircraft Electrical Systems
metadata.description: Micro-training generated for W3: Electrical Fundamentals & Aircraft Electrical Systems

blocks.content: Use V=IR relationships to reason about current/voltage/resistance changes.

items.definition: Current (I) equals voltage (V) divided by resistance (R): I = V / R. This fundamental law relates the three primary quantities in any DC circuit.
items.analogy: Think of a garden hose: voltage is water pressure, resistance is how narrow the hose is, and current is the flow rate — more pressure with the same hose gives you more flow.

items.definition: Voltage equals current multiplied by resistance: V = I x R. This form is used when current and resistance are known and voltage is the unknown quantity.
items.analogy: Voltage is the 'push' a circuit needs. The more current you want to force through a given resistance, the more voltage you must apply — they multiply together.

items.definition: Applying I = V / R: with 24 volts and 12 ohms of resistance, the circuit current is 2 amperes. This is a direct application of Ohm's Law.
items.analogy: If a water pipe delivers 24 units of pressure through a valve with 12 units of restriction, the flow rate is exactly 2 units — the restriction cuts the flow proportionally.

items.definition: I = V / R = 12V / 6Ω = 2 amps. This straightforward application of Ohm's Law confirms that a 12-volt supply drives 2 amperes through 6 ohms of total circuit resistance.
items.analogy: A 12-unit pressure source pushing through a 6-unit restriction delivers exactly 2 units of flow — halving the resistance compared to 12 ohms doubles the 1-amp result you would expect there.

items.definition: Using R = V / I: with 14 volts across a component and 7 amperes through it, the resistance is 2 ohms. This form of Ohm's Law identifies unknown resistance from measured quantities.
items.analogy: If you know how hard you pushed (voltage) and how fast the result came (current), you can calculate how much friction was in the system (resistance).

items.definition: When resistance is held constant, current is directly proportional to voltage. If voltage doubles, current doubles: I = V / R means I scales linearly with V.
items.analogy: Doubling the water pressure in a pipe with the same valve opening forces twice as much water through — the flow is directly proportional to pressure.

items.definition: When voltage is constant, current is inversely proportional to resistance (I = V / R). Doubling resistance halves current; halving resistance doubles current.
items.analogy: If you partially close a valve in a pipe while keeping the same upstream pressure, flow rate drops — double the restriction, half the flow.

items.definition: When resistance is constant, voltage is directly proportional to current (V = I x R). Doubling the current through a fixed resistance doubles the voltage across it.
items.analogy: Double the flow through the same pipe restriction and the back-pressure (voltage) doubles — the restriction (resistance) amplifies the pressure effect proportionally.

blocks.question: Which equation correctly states Ohm's Law when solving for current?
choices: I = V / R
I = V + R
I = R / V
I = V x R
blocks.feedback: Ohm's Law states that current (I) equals voltage (V) divided by resistance (R): I = V / R. The other forms — V = I x R and R = V / I — are algebraic rearrangements of the same relationship. A common error is inverting the fraction, giving R / V instead of V / R.

blocks.question: Which equation correctly states Ohm's Law when voltage is the unknown?
choices: V = I + R
V = I x R
V = I / R
V = R - I
blocks.feedback: V = I x R is the voltage form of Ohm's Law. It is used to predict the voltage developed across a known resistance when current is given — for example, calculating voltage drop across a wire or connector resistance.

blocks.question: A circuit is powered by a 24-volt battery and has a total resistance of 12 ohms. What is the current flowing through the circuit?
choices: 0.5 amps
12 amps
24 amps
2 amps
blocks.feedback: Using I = V / R: I = 24V / 12Ω = 2 amps. Multiplying voltage by resistance (24 x 12 = 288) or confusing units are common errors. Always divide voltage by resistance to find current.

blocks.question: A 12-volt battery is the sole power source in a circuit with a total resistance of 6 ohms. What is the circuit current?
choices: 0.5 amps
6 amps
72 amps
2 amps
blocks.feedback: I = V / R = 12V / 6Ω = 2 amps. This is a direct Ohm's Law calculation. Selecting 6 amps is a common error where the student uses the resistance value as the current answer. Selecting 0.5 amps results from dividing R by V instead of V by R.

blocks.question: A multimeter measures 14 volts across a circuit element, and a clamp meter reads 7 amps through the same element. What is the element's resistance?
choices: 98 ohms
0.5 ohms
7 ohms
2 ohms
blocks.feedback: R = V / I = 14V / 7A = 2 ohms. This rearrangement of Ohm's Law is used when both voltage and current can be measured but resistance is not directly readable. It is commonly used to verify connector and switch contact resistance in aircraft wiring audits.

blocks.question: A circuit has a fixed resistance of 10 ohms. The voltage is increased from 12V to 24V. What happens to the circuit current?
choices: Current doubles because current is directly proportional to voltage
Current stays the same because resistance did not change
Current is halved because voltage and current are inversely related
Current quadruples because power increases with the square of voltage
blocks.feedback: Using I = V / R: at 12V, I = 1.2A; at 24V, I = 2.4A — exactly double. When resistance is constant, current is directly proportional to voltage. Doubling voltage doubles current. This linear relationship is central to predicting how a circuit responds to bus voltage changes.

blocks.question: A 28V circuit normally carries 4 amps through a 7-ohm load. The load is replaced with a 14-ohm component. The voltage stays at 28V. What is the new current?
choices: 8 amps — doubling resistance doubles current
2 amps — doubling resistance halves current
4 amps — current is determined solely by voltage
1 amp — current is quartered when resistance doubles
blocks.feedback: At 7Ω: I = 28/7 = 4A. At 14Ω: I = 28/14 = 2A. Doubling resistance halves the current when voltage is constant — an inverse relationship. This is why an undersized resistor (lower R) allows more current than intended and can overheat.

blocks.question: Current through a 10-ohm resistor increases from 1 amp to 2 amps. What happens to the voltage across the resistor?
choices: Voltage decreases from 10V to 5V
Voltage stays constant at 10V
Voltage increases from 10V to 100V
Voltage increases from 10V to 20V
blocks.feedback: V = I x R. At 1A: V = 1 x 10 = 10V. At 2A: V = 2 x 10 = 20V. The voltage doubles because current doubled with resistance held constant. This linear proportionality is a direct consequence of Ohm's Law.

blocks.content: Use P=V×I and interpret power in simple electrical scenarios.

items.term: Power formula: P = V x I
items.definition: Electrical power in watts equals voltage multiplied by current: P = V x I. At 12 volts and 2 amperes, the power is 24 watts.
items.analogy: Power is work rate — voltage is like the height of a waterfall (potential energy per unit), current is the volume of water flowing, and power is how fast total energy is delivered.

items.definition: P = V x I = 28V x 25A = 700 watts. Calculating bus power is essential in aircraft electrical system load analysis to ensure generator capacity is not exceeded.
items.analogy: A 28V bus drawing 25A is like 700 one-watt bulbs all lit simultaneously — a significant load that must be accounted for in the aircraft's electrical budget.

items.definition: Power = V x I. If both voltage and current double simultaneously, power quadruples: (2V) x (2I) = 4(V x I). Each quantity doubling multiplies the power by its own factor.
items.analogy: If you double both the flow rate and the pressure in a hydraulic system, the total power (rate of work) increases by four — each factor independently multiplies the result.

blocks.question: An avionics unit is powered by a 12-volt bus and draws 2 amperes. What is the power consumption of the unit?
choices: 24 watts
6 watts
10 watts
144 watts
blocks.feedback: P = V x I = 12V x 2A = 24 watts. Understanding power consumption is essential for electrical load analysis — ensuring that installed avionics do not exceed the aircraft's generator and bus capacity.

blocks.question: During a load analysis, the total current draw from a 28VDC bus is measured at 25 amps. What is the total electrical power being consumed?
choices: 700 watts
196 watts
53 watts
25 watts
blocks.feedback: P = V x I = 28V x 25A = 700 watts. This is a standard aircraft electrical load calculation. Most general aviation alternators are rated in watts or amps at 28V; knowing the total load in watts allows direct comparison to the alternator's rated output.

blocks.question: A circuit originally operates at 6 volts and 2 amps. Both the voltage and the current are then doubled to 12 volts and 4 amps. What happens to the power dissipation?
choices: It doubles from 12W to 24W
It triples from 12W to 36W
It increases by 4W, from 12W to 16W
It quadruples from 12W to 48W
blocks.feedback: Original power: P = 6V x 2A = 12W. New power: P = 12V x 4A = 48W. That is exactly 4 times the original — power quadruples when both voltage and current double. This demonstrates why overcurrent faults are destructive: heat in a conductor scales with I², and if voltage also rises, power scales even faster.

items.definition: In a series circuit, total resistance equals the sum of all individual resistances: Rt = R1 + R2 + R3. Because current has only one path, every resistor adds to the total opposition.
items.analogy: Like driving through multiple toll booths in a row — each one adds delay to your total trip time, and you cannot bypass any of them.

items.definition: Using 1/Rt = 1/10000 + 1/1000 + 1/500 = 0.0001 + 0.001 + 0.002 = 0.0021 → Rt = 1/0.0021 ≈ 476 ohms. The result is always less than the smallest branch (500 ohms).
items.analogy: Three traffic lanes of different widths merge into one — a very wide lane (low resistance, 500Ω) dominates the total flow capacity. The narrowest lanes add a little but the total is controlled mostly by the widest.

items.definition: In a parallel circuit, total current from the source equals the sum of all individual branch currents: It = I1 + I2 + I3. Each branch draws independently, and the source must supply all of them.
items.analogy: Like multiple faucets on the same water main — each open faucet draws its own flow, and the main supply must deliver the sum of all flows simultaneously.

items.definition: Adding resistors in parallel always reduces total circuit resistance because each new branch provides an additional current path. Total parallel resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistor.
items.analogy: Opening extra checkout lanes at a store reduces the total wait time — more lanes (paths) mean the total flow capacity increases, so the overall resistance to traffic decreases.

items.definition: In a parallel circuit, each load has its own independent path to the power source. If one branch opens (bulb burns out), the remaining branches continue to receive full voltage and remain operational.
items.analogy: Like outlets on a wall — if one lamp blows a bulb, the other plugged-in devices keep working because each has its own independent connection to the panel.

blocks.question: Three resistors of 5 ohms, 8 ohms, and 7 ohms are connected in series. What is the total resistance of the circuit?
choices: 20 ohms
2.2 ohms
5 ohms
280 ohms
blocks.feedback: Series resistance: Rt = R1 + R2 + R3 = 5 + 8 + 7 = 20 ohms. In a series circuit, current flows through all resistors in sequence and each one adds to the total. The result is always larger than any single resistor in the string.

blocks.question: Three resistors — 10,000 ohms, 1,000 ohms, and 500 ohms — are wired in parallel. What is the approximate total resistance?
choices: 476 ohms
11,500 ohms
3,833 ohms
500 ohms
blocks.feedback: 1/Rt = 1/10000 + 1/1000 + 1/500 = 0.0001 + 0.001 + 0.002 = 0.0021 → Rt ≈ 476 ohms. Total parallel resistance is always less than the smallest branch. Note that the 10kΩ resistor contributes very little compared to the 500Ω branch — the low-resistance branch dominates in parallel circuits.

blocks.question: A 28VDC bus feeds three parallel avionics loads drawing 3A, 2A, and 1A respectively. What is the total current the bus must supply?
choices: 6 amps
2 amps
1 amp
3 amps
blocks.feedback: It = I1 + I2 + I3 = 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 amps. In a parallel circuit, each branch draws its own current from the source, and the total is the sum of all branches. Knowing the total current is essential for sizing fuses, circuit breakers, and bus wiring.

blocks.question: A 100-ohm resistor is connected across a circuit. A second 100-ohm resistor is added in parallel. What happens to the total resistance?
choices: It increases to 200 ohms because resistance adds in parallel
It decreases to 10 ohms because the values multiply in parallel
It stays at 100 ohms because the resistors are identical
It decreases to 50 ohms because parallel paths reduce total resistance
blocks.feedback: For two equal resistors in parallel: Rt = R/2 = 100/2 = 50 ohms. Adding any parallel branch always reduces total resistance — it never stays the same or increases. The general rule: Rt is always less than the smallest branch resistor in a parallel combination.

blocks.question: An aircraft's navigation lights are wired in parallel across the 28VDC bus. One bulb burns out, creating an open in that branch. What happens to the other navigation lights?
choices: All lights go out because the circuit is broken
The remaining lights glow dimmer due to reduced total resistance
The bus voltage drops and a circuit breaker trips
The remaining lights stay at full brightness because each branch is independent
blocks.feedback: In a parallel circuit, each branch has direct access to the full supply voltage. An open in one branch only stops current in that branch — the other branches are unaffected and continue operating at full voltage. This is why safety-critical aircraft lights use parallel wiring rather than series.

blocks.content: Explain overcurrent protection purpose and basic device behavior.

items.definition: Fuses and circuit breakers protect wiring and equipment from overcurrent. When current exceeds the rated value, they interrupt the circuit before the wire overheats and starts a fire. They protect the WIRE, not the equipment — sized to the wire's current capacity.
items.analogy: Like a pressure relief valve on a boiler — it blows before the boiler does, protecting the more expensive and dangerous component.

items.definition: A fuse contains a metal element that melts when current exceeds its rated value, permanently opening the circuit. Unlike a circuit breaker, a fuse cannot be reset — it must be replaced. It protects the wiring from overheating by interrupting excessive current.
items.analogy: Like a one-time safety link in a chain — it breaks before the chain does, but has to be replaced after.

blocks.question: What is the primary purpose of fuses and circuit breakers in an aircraft electrical system?
choices: To regulate voltage to connected avionics
To protect wiring and equipment from overcurrent that could cause fire or damage
To filter noise from the electrical bus
To disconnect the battery during engine shutdown
blocks.feedback: Fuses and breakers are overcurrent protection — they protect the wire from carrying more current than its insulation can safely handle. Wire insulation failures from overcurrent are a primary cause of aircraft electrical fires.

blocks.question: What happens inside a fuse when current exceeds its rated value?
choices: It trips a mechanical switch that can be reset
Its element melts, permanently opening the circuit to protect the wiring
It reduces the circuit voltage to safe levels
It redirects excess current to a ground bus
blocks.feedback: A fuse's metal element melts when overcurrent occurs, permanently breaking the circuit. This protects the wiring from carrying current levels that would overheat the insulation. The fuse must then be replaced — it cannot be reset like a breaker.

blocks.content: Describe electrical buses and distribution concepts in aircraft.

items.definition: An electrical bus is a common conductive distribution point connected to one or more power sources (battery, alternator) and multiple loads (avionics, lights, systems). All loads connected to the bus share the same voltage source.
items.analogy: Like a power strip — one plug into the wall (power source), many devices plugged in (loads), all sharing the same supply.

items.definition: The DC electrical system supplies power to all electrically-powered equipment: avionics (radios, navigation, flight instruments), lighting, ignition systems, fuel pumps, and other electrical loads — during all phases of flight from pre-start through shutdown.
items.analogy: The aircraft's DC system is like the bloodstream of the aircraft's electrical life — everything that needs power gets it from here.

items.definition: The DC electrical system in a GA aircraft powers: avionics (radios, navigation equipment), lighting (position lights, landing lights, interior), ignition systems, electric fuel pump, and any other electrically-operated equipment.
items.analogy: The DC system is the electrical utility network of the aircraft — like the electrical panel in a house powering everything from the refrigerator to the lights.

blocks.question: What is an aircraft electrical bus?
choices: A dedicated cable that connects the battery directly to each load
A protective device that interrupts power during faults
A voltage regulation device for sensitive avionics
A common distribution point that supplies power from one or more sources to multiple loads
blocks.feedback: A bus is a distribution node: power comes in from sources (battery, alternator) and goes out to all connected loads. Multiple buses allow circuit separation — essential loads on one bus, non-essential on another — for fault tolerance.

blocks.question: What is the primary purpose of an aircraft's DC electrical system?
choices: To convert AC power from the alternator into usable DC
To supply power to avionics, lights, ignition, fuel systems, and electrical equipment during all phases of operation
To charge the battery only when the alternator is operating at cruise RPM
To distribute power solely to flight-critical instruments
blocks.feedback: The DC electrical system serves as the backbone of all electrical power distribution — from pre-start checks through engine shutdown. It powers both flight-critical and non-critical electrical loads at all times.

blocks.question: In a general aviation aircraft, what does the DC electrical system primarily power?
choices: Only the avionics and radios
Only flight-critical instruments and the battery charger
Avionics, lighting, ignition systems, and other electrical equipment
Only lighting and the electric fuel pump
blocks.feedback: The DC system is comprehensive — it powers all electrical loads: avionics, all lighting systems, ignition, fuel pump, and miscellaneous electrical equipment. GA aircraft have very few non-electrical systems.

blocks.content: Describe battery function and bonding/grounding basics.

items.term: Aircraft battery — role in DC system
items.definition: The battery is the initial power source: it powers avionics, fuel pump, and starter motor during engine starting. Once the engine is running and up to speed, the alternator (or generator) takes over as the primary power source and recharges the battery.
items.analogy: Like a car's starter battery — it gets the engine going, then the alternator takes over to run everything and recharge it.

items.definition: Always remove the NEGATIVE (ground) cable FIRST when disconnecting a battery. If a tool touches the airframe while removing the positive cable with the negative already disconnected, no circuit is completed — no spark. Removing positive first risks a short if the tool contacts the airframe.
items.analogy: Like turning off the water main before disconnecting a pipe fitting — remove the source of danger before handling the connection.

items.definition: A bonding jumper creates a low-resistance electrical path between a component and the aircraft structure. Three purposes: (1) current return path (grounding), (2) lightning protection (provides controlled dissipation path), (3) EMI reduction (prevents static buildup and ground loops).
items.analogy: Like a bridge between two islands — it ensures current can flow freely between them rather than building up on one side.

items.term: Bonding jumper — current return and static discharge
items.definition: Bonding jumpers provide two key functions: (1) current return — the low-resistance path for DC current to return from loads back to the battery/bus through the airframe, and (2) static discharge — preventing static charge buildup that could cause interference or spark ignition near fuel.
items.analogy: Like a dedicated return lane on a highway — it ensures the traffic (current) that went out can efficiently come back.

blocks.question: What is the battery's role in a DC aircraft electrical system during engine start?
choices: It regulates alternator output voltage
It filters noise from the electrical bus
It stores excess power generated during cruise flight only
It is the initial power source before the alternator comes online
blocks.feedback: The battery provides all electrical power during engine starting — before the alternator reaches its operating speed and output voltage. Once the alternator is online, it becomes the primary source and recharges the battery.

blocks.question: What is the correct first step when disconnecting an aircraft battery?
choices: Remove the ground (negative) cable first
Remove the positive (hot) cable first
Remove both cables simultaneously
Turn off the master switch, then remove either cable
blocks.feedback: Always remove negative first. With the ground disconnected, the positive terminal is no longer connected to the return path — accidental contact of the positive terminal with the airframe won't cause a short. Removing positive first with negative still connected creates a short circuit risk.

blocks.question: What is the primary purpose of bonding jumpers in an aircraft electrical system?
choices: To carry main power from the bus to avionics LRUs
To provide a low-resistance path between components and structure for grounding, lightning protection, and EMI reduction
To carry return current only from AC systems
To mechanically secure avionics equipment to the aircraft rack
blocks.feedback: Bonding jumpers serve three critical electrical functions: they provide the current return path (ground), they give lightning energy a controlled low-resistance path to the airframe (rather than through avionics), and they reduce EMI by equalizing potentials between components.

blocks.question: In a single-wire aircraft electrical system, what role does the airframe play, and how does a bonding jumper enable it?
choices: The airframe carries positive current; bonding connects positive terminals to structure
The airframe serves as the negative current return conductor; bonding jumpers provide the low-resistance connection from components to structure
The airframe insulates components from ground; bonding jumpers add resistance to prevent faults
The airframe is the positive bus; bonding jumpers connect it to the battery negative
blocks.feedback: Most GA aircraft use single-wire electrical systems where the airframe IS the negative return conductor. Bonding jumpers connect avionics and components to the airframe so current can return to the battery. Without proper bonding, return current has no path and equipment won't function.

blocks.content: Introduction to Power generation and regulation
Describe alternator/generator basics and voltage regulator function.

items.definition: Alternators are preferred in modern aircraft because: (1) they produce usable charging voltage at low RPM (including idle), and (2) they are lighter than generators of equivalent output. Generators require higher RPM to produce the same output and are heavier.
items.analogy: Like a newer, more efficient engine that makes full power from idle rather than needing high RPM to get going.

items.definition: The voltage regulator controls alternator or generator field current to maintain a consistent output voltage (typically 28V ±0.5V in aircraft). Without it, alternator output would vary with RPM and load, potentially overcharging the battery or under-powering avionics.
items.analogy: Like a thermostat for electrical voltage — it constantly adjusts to keep output steady regardless of engine speed or load.

items.definition: Capacitors and inductors (chokes) are used to filter alternator-generated electrical noise from the DC bus. Capacitors shunt high-frequency noise to ground; inductors block high-frequency noise from passing through. Together they form a low-pass filter keeping the bus clean for sensitive avionics.
items.analogy: Like a water filter — lets clean water (clean DC) through while trapping particles (electrical noise).

blocks.question: Why are alternators preferred over generators in modern aircraft DC electrical systems?
choices: They produce AC power directly usable by avionics
They produce usable output at lower RPM and are lighter weight
They require no voltage regulator for output control
They have higher internal resistance which protects against surges
blocks.feedback: The two key advantages: (1) alternators charge at low RPM — including idle — whereas generators need higher RPM to produce charging voltage; (2) alternators are lighter for equivalent output. Both matter greatly in aviation.

blocks.question: Which component is responsible for maintaining consistent alternator output voltage in an aircraft DC electrical system?
choices: Main bus tie
Voltage regulator
Battery contactor
Rectifier diode assembly
blocks.feedback: The voltage regulator monitors alternator output and adjusts field excitation to maintain the setpoint voltage. It compensates for changes in engine speed and electrical load to keep bus voltage stable.

blocks.question: Which components are used to filter and suppress alternator noise in an aircraft DC electrical system?
choices: Resistors and fuses
Voltage regulators and bus relays
Capacitors and inductors (chokes)
Diodes and Zener references
blocks.feedback: Capacitors and inductors form a filter network on the alternator output. Capacitors shunt high-frequency noise to ground; inductors block noise from reaching the bus. This protects avionics from electrical interference generated by the alternator.

blocks.content: Explain AC waveform/frequency and basic reactance/transformer concepts (entry level).

items.definition: Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz). One hertz equals one complete AC cycle per second. Aircraft AC systems typically operate at 400 Hz; household power in the US is 60 Hz.
items.analogy: Hertz is to AC cycles what RPM is to engine rotation — it counts how many times something completes a full cycle every second.

items.definition: Capacitance is measured in farads (F). Because one farad is extremely large, practical avionics capacitors are rated in microfarads (µF, 10⁻⁶ F) or picofarads (pF, 10⁻¹² F). Microfarads are most common in avionics power filtering circuits.
items.analogy: The farad is like measuring road distance in light-years — technically correct but impractically large. Avionics engineers use microfarads for the same reason road builders use miles or kilometers.

items.definition: Inductive reactance (XL) is the opposition an inductor presents to AC current flow. It is measured in ohms and increases proportionally with frequency: XL = 2πfL. Higher frequency → higher reactance → less AC current through the inductor.
items.analogy: An inductor resists changes in current. At higher frequency, current changes direction faster, so the inductor opposes it more strongly — like a shock absorber that stiffens up at higher vibration frequencies.

items.definition: The primary advantage of AC in aircraft is the ability to use transformers to step voltage up or down. Higher voltage means lower current for the same power (P = V x I), which allows smaller, lighter wiring — critical in weight-sensitive aircraft.
items.analogy: High-tension power lines carry electricity cross-country at very high voltage and low current, using thinner wire than would be needed at household voltage. Aircraft AC systems exploit the same physics.

items.definition: A single-phase AC waveform is a sinusoidal (sine wave) curve that rises above zero to a positive peak, returns through zero, falls to a negative peak, and returns to zero — completing one full cycle at the system frequency.
items.analogy: Imagine a cork bobbing on ocean waves — it continuously rises above and dips below the calm waterline in a smooth, repeating pattern. The voltage does the same around the zero-volt line.

items.definition: A transformer transfers electrical power from one AC circuit to another through electromagnetic induction, simultaneously stepping voltage up or down based on the turns ratio of the primary and secondary windings. Transformers only work with AC.
items.analogy: A transformer is like a mechanical gear system for electrical power — it trades off voltage for current (or current for voltage) to match the 'gear ratio' of the winding turns, just as gears trade off speed for torque.

items.definition: A frequency counter or calibrated oscilloscope are the correct instruments to verify that an AC alternator is producing the correct output frequency (typically 400 Hz) during bench testing.
items.analogy: Like using a stopwatch to verify the beat rate of a metronome — you need an instrument specifically designed to count cycles per second, not one that just measures magnitude.

blocks.question: The frequency of an AC electrical system is expressed in which unit?
choices: Watts (W)
Amperes (A)
Hertz (Hz)
Ohms (Ω)
blocks.feedback: Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), which represents the number of complete cycles per second. Watts measure power, amperes measure current, and ohms measure resistance — none of these units describe how many times per second an AC waveform completes a cycle.

blocks.question: What is the SI unit of capacitance, and what smaller denomination is most commonly used when specifying capacitors in avionics circuits?
choices: Henry (H); millihenries are most common in avionics
Farad (F); microfarads (µF) are most common in avionics
Ohm (Ω); milliohms are most common in avionics
Coulomb (C); microcoulombs are most common in avionics
blocks.feedback: Capacitance is measured in farads (F). The farad is too large for practical components, so avionics capacitors are typically specified in microfarads (µF). For high-frequency RF circuits, picofarads (pF) are used. Henries measure inductance, ohms measure resistance, and coulombs measure charge — not capacitance.

blocks.question: Which statement correctly describes inductive reactance?
choices: It is the opposition to DC current flow by an inductor, measured in henries
It is the opposition to AC current flow by an inductor, measured in ohms and increasing with frequency
It is the opposition to current flow by a capacitor, measured in ohms and decreasing with frequency
It is the total opposition to current flow in any circuit, combining resistance and reactance
blocks.feedback: Inductive reactance (XL) is the opposition to AC current flow produced by an inductor, measured in ohms, with the value increasing as frequency rises (XL = 2πfL). The henry is the unit of inductance itself, not reactance. Capacitive reactance decreases with frequency (the opposite behavior). Impedance combines both resistance and reactance.

blocks.question: What is the primary advantage of using an AC electrical system in aircraft compared to a purely DC system?
choices: AC is safer to work on than DC systems of equivalent voltage
AC can be stored in batteries more efficiently than DC
AC systems allow transformers to change voltage levels, enabling lighter wiring for high-power loads
AC eliminates the need for circuit breakers in aircraft wiring systems
blocks.feedback: The key advantage of AC is transformer compatibility. Transformers can step voltage up or down, allowing high-power loads to be powered at high voltage and low current — which means thinner, lighter wiring. DC voltage cannot be changed by a simple transformer; you need electronic converters instead, which are heavier and less efficient for large power levels.

blocks.question: How is the voltage waveform of a single-phase AC electrical system best described?
choices: A constant DC level interrupted by brief spikes
A square wave toggling between a fixed positive and fixed negative voltage
A sinusoidal curve that smoothly alternates above and below zero voltage
A triangular wave that linearly ramps between peak and zero
blocks.feedback: A single-phase AC waveform is sinusoidal — it follows a sine function over time, continuously and smoothly alternating between positive and negative values. One complete trip from zero, to positive peak, back through zero, to negative peak, and back to zero constitutes one cycle. This shape results directly from the physics of rotating electromagnetic alternators.

blocks.question: How does a transformer transfer power from its primary circuit to its secondary circuit?
choices: By direct electrical conduction through a common wire connecting both windings
Through electromagnetic induction, where the AC in the primary winding creates a changing magnetic field that induces voltage in the secondary winding
By converting AC to DC in the primary and regenerating AC in the secondary
By storing energy in a magnetic core and releasing it at a different voltage during the off cycle
blocks.feedback: Transformers work by electromagnetic induction. The AC primary current creates a changing magnetic flux in the core. This changing flux induces a voltage in the secondary winding proportional to the turns ratio. There is no direct electrical connection between primary and secondary windings — power is coupled magnetically. This galvanic isolation is a secondary benefit used in avionics power supplies.

blocks.question: A technician needs to confirm that a repaired aircraft AC alternator is producing the correct output frequency before returning it to service. Which instrument is most appropriate for this verification?
choices: A standard AC voltmeter to measure output voltage magnitude
A frequency counter or calibrated oscilloscope to measure output frequency
An ammeter to measure current output at full load
A digital multimeter set to resistance to verify winding continuity
blocks.feedback: Frequency must be verified with a frequency counter or oscilloscope. A voltmeter confirms output amplitude but gives no frequency information. An ammeter verifies current capacity. Resistance measurement is useful for winding checks but does not verify operational frequency. Only a frequency counter or oscilloscope directly measures Hz.
